newsitem.title: GERMANY: German miners mass again to protest at subsidy cut.
newsitem.headline: German miners mass again to protest at subsidy cut.

text.p: Thousands of German miners gathered in Bonn's government quarter for a third day of protest on Wednesday despite Chancellor Helmut Kohl's warning that talks would not be held in a climate of intimidation.

Coal miners' representatives from Saar state on the French border said they expected around 10,000 pit workers to attend a rally at 10.30 a.m. (0930 GMT) in the area of Bonn which the protesters have virtually besieged since Monday.

On Tuesday, a demonstration by miners from Germany's Ruhr valley coal-and-steel heartland spilled over briefly into violence, prompting Kohl to postpone talks with the miners' union at short notice until Thursday.
Those miners heeded an appeal from union leader Hans Berger to leave Bonn, but no sooner had they gone than another 3,000 or so Saar miners arrived to keep up a night-time vigil.

They maintained a blockade of Bonn's main drive, causing morning traffic chaos, and kept up a siege of the headquarters of the free-market Free Democrats (FDP), Kohl's junior coalition partners who are the main force behind the subsidy cuts.
Unlike the Ruhr valley miners, many of those who came from the Saar were equipped with tents and sleeping bags.

"We're staying here until Thursday when a decision has to be made," said Ruediger Heinze, 36, from the town of Dinslaken, one of the miners who spent the night camping in tents outside Bonn's art museum or huddling in an underground railway station.
"We're only going home when we have a clear answer from the government on how much money we're going to get...And we're not planning to go home empty-handed."
The Ruhr valley miners also planned to continue their demonstrations back at home on Wednesday, with between 5,000 and 10,000 expected to turn out at a rally at the Werne colliery.
Miners in Germany's 18 pits downed their tools on Friday after Bonn said it would cut subsidies to 3.8 billion marks ($2.2 billion) by 2005 instead of to a promised 6.5 billion marks.

Bonn argues that at time of severe budget strain, it can no longer afford to pay over nine billion marks a year to compensate users for a domestic coal price which is over three times the world market price.
But mining union IG Bergbau says the plans will force 10 pits to close by 2005, make 50,000 miners redundant and cause a further 70,000 related job losses in already depressed areas.

The Berliner Zeitung daily, citing government sources, reported that Bonn was now prepared to give a little ground to the miners by offering an additional 300 million marks a year in payments until 2000.
Kohl's Chancellery Minister Friedrich Bohl told ZDF television late on Tuesday that the government was standing by its plan, but he added that he saw the potential for an agreement with the union.
FDP leader Wolfgang Gerhardt told German Radio the government officials might be prepared to be more flexible on the timetable for phasing out the subsidies.
The opposition Social Democrats (SPD), who rule the two main coal mining states, have strongly backed the miners.
But they said for the first time on Wednesday they would not maintain a boycott of talks with the government on tax reform, even if Kohl failed to make a satisfactory offer to the pit workers.

"We are committed to help the miners but we are also committed to help other unemployed workers including those who are currently demonstrating in the construction industry," SPD party manager Franz Muentefering told German Radio.
